query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a ~5 µm thick, nano-laminated, oxide-based coating (e.g., PVD-applied CrN/Al2O3) on a CoCrFeNi alloy will promote the in situ formation of a stable, self-regenerating lubricious tribo-oxide layer during sliding, thereby maintaining low friction and reduced wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Bare CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting acceptable room‐temperature friction performance but suffering from high friction and wear rates at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled and unstable oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a ~5 µm thick, adherent oxide-based coating using a process that includes moderate substrate preheating (~300 °C), controlled reactive gas flow to achieve a stoichiometric, nano-laminated CrN/Al2O3 structure, and a post-deposition annealing step to stabilize the interface.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests conducted in air, over a temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C, under moderate contact stresses representative of service loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered nano-laminated coating, which is designed to form and sustain a continuous, lubricious tribo-oxide (e.g., protective Cr2O3 and Al2O3 phases) at the sliding interface during frictional heating.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, frictional heating triggers controlled oxidation within the coating, generating a stable oxide glaze that acts as a low shear strength, self-replenishing lubricant. This protective layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the entire temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated alloy will consistently display lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates over the full temperature range (25–800 °C) due to the presence and stability of the tribo-oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Uncoated, bare CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which lacks a controlled surface architecture and shows degradation of tribological performance at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Valid under dry sliding conditions in air with typical contact stresses; the intervention is expected to perform within the temperature boundary of 25 °C to 800 °C under service-like loads.
generation.uncertainty: Results may vary depending on the long-term adhesion and durability of the coating under repeated thermal cycling and severe sliding conditions, and the optimum coating composition and processing parameters may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the PVD-deposited CrN/Al2O3 nano-laminated coating (with proper preheating and post-deposition annealing) and one set without any coating (baseline). Conduct systematic dry sliding tests at multiple key temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) under identical contact stresses in air. Characterize the sliding interfaces using in situ friction measurements, wear track profilometry, scanning electron microscopy, and spectroscopy to assess the formation and stability of the tribo-oxide layer.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction during sliding
Wear rate (volumetric material loss) from profilometry
Microstructural and phase analysis of the worn surface via SEM/TEM and XPS/Raman spectroscopy
Adhesion and integrity assessment of the coating pre- and post-testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, across the temperature range, the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20%) in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the uncoated baseline, or if the anticipated stable and continuous tribo-oxide layer is not confirmed by microstructural analysis.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

decision.trend: Beginning around 2017, researchers exploring CoCrFeNi-based or related FCC-type high-entropy alloys for tribology initially focused on adding oxide dispersions (e.g., Y2O3) to enhance mechanical properties and wear resistance near room temperature (PMC5706259). Follow-up studies applied spark plasma sintering to Al-containing and W-alloyed CoCrFeNi variants, revealing that high-temperature sliding performance often benefited from the formation of protective oxide layers but depended heavily on specific compositional modifications (PMC7515071, PMC8470387). Parallel work on CoCrFeMnNi in vacuum demonstrated promising low friction but under conditions very different from real-service elevated-temperature environments (PMC7311485). More recently, development of nanohierarchical microstructures and compositionally modulated layers has proven effective at delivering excellent wear resistance from room temperature up to 800 °C, although these solutions involve re-engineering the alloy or building novel multiphase architectures (PMC10241162). Overall, the field has shown that carefully engineered oxide tribofilms or multiphase microstructures can help reduce friction and wear at high temperatures, but a robust, single-step approach to enable a baseline CoCrFeNi alloy to reliably maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: Despite success with compositional adjustments and multicomponent oxide layers, a straightforward, single-solution method to achieve stable, low-friction and low-wear performance over the full 25–800 °C range in a baseline CoCrFeNi alloy is still lacking. Compositional modifications can solve some of the high-temperature tribological instability but often complicate room-temperature performance. A unifying approach that exploits surface or interface engineering—rather than bulk re-alloying—has yet to be firmly established.
decision.lever: Deposit a ~5 µm thick, adherent oxide-based coating (e.g., a PVD-applied CrN/Al2O3 or similar nano-laminated tuck-in layer) designed to form and sustain a lubricious tribo-oxide at high temperatures (up to 800 °C). Process parameters include moderate substrate preheating (~300 °C), controlled reactive gas flow for stoichiometric oxide formation, and final post-deposition annealing to stabilize the coating and to ensure good bonding.
decision.why: Recent efforts highlight that oxide-scale formation is key to robust high-temperature tribological performance (as in PMC7515071 and PMC10241162). Rather than modifying bulk alloy composition, an engineered oxide coating can provide a self-regenerating, thermally stable surface “glaze” that protects against wear and maintains low friction from room temperature to 800 °C (including typical contact stresses in sliding). This approach directly addresses the open question of bridging consistent low-friction behavior across a wide temperature range with minimal changes to the baseline CoCrFeNi matrix.
